title: One Thousand and One Nights
description: Collection of Middle Eastern folk tales
wiki_lead:
One Thousand and One Nights or The Thousand and One Nights (Persian: هزار و یک شب) is a collection of Middle Eastern folktales compiled in the Arabic language during the Islamic Golden Age. It is often known in English as The Arabian Nights, from the first English-language edition (c. 1706–1721), which rendered the title as The Arabian Nights' Entertainments.
The work was collected over many centuries by various authors, translators, and scholars across West Asia, Central Asia, South Asia, and North Africa.  Some tales trace their roots back to ancient and medieval Persian, Arabic, and Mesopotamian literature. Most tales, however, were originally folk stories from the Abbasid and Mamluk eras, while others, especially the frame story, are drawn from the Pahlavi Persian work Hezār Afsān (Persian: هزار افسان, lit. 'A Thousand Tales'), which in turn relied partly on Indian elements.
If there was ever a canonical text with all the stories in a specific order, that text is no longer extant. But remaining editions of the Nights have some things in common, including the story's framing device. In the frame story, the ruler Shahryar is told the tales by his wife Scheherazade, with one tale told over each night of storytelling. The stories proceed from this original tale; some are framed within other tales, while some are self-contained. Some editions contain only a few hundred nights of storytelling, while others include 1001 or more. The bulk of the text is in prose, although verse is occasionally used for songs and riddles and to express heightened emotion. Most of the poems are single couplets or quatrains, although some are longer.
Some of the stories commonly associated with the Arabian Nights—particularly "Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp" and "Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves"—were not part of the collection in the original Arabic versions, but were instead added to the collection by French translator Antoine Galland after he heard them from Syrian writer Hanna Diyab during the latter's visit to Paris in 1709. Other stories, such as "The Seven Voyages of Sinbad the Sailor", had an independent existence before being added to the collection in later manuscripts and translations.

Some editions contain only a few hundred nights of storytelling, while others include 1001 or more. Most of the poems are single couplets or quatrains, although some are longer.

Other stories, such as "The Seven Voyages of Sinbad the Sailor", had an independent existence before being added to the collection in later manuscripts and translations.


Synopsis


The Frame Story
The main frame story concerns Shahriyâr, a king who ruled an empire that stretched from Persia to India. The story begins with Shâhzamân, the King of Samarkand and brother of Shahriyâr, setting out on a journey to visit his brother at his palace. Early in the preparations, he remembers that he's left something inside his own palace, and returns to retrieve it—only to find that his wife has been having sex with a black cook in their own bed. He kills them both, and continues on his journey, keeping the event a secret. In the court of his brother, Shâhzamân was overcome with grief and didn't eat.
Then Shâhzamân finds that his brother's own wife, as well as his numerous slave girls, have been engaging in secret orgies with black men. He shares his discovery with his brother. 
In their bitterness and grief, both brothers abandoned the kingdom to roam the world. They were sleeping by the seashore, when a jinn appears suddenly. The brothers hide and see that the jinn is carrying a chest, where he keeps a captive woman. The jinn goes to sleep and the woman discovers the brothers and threatens them with awaking the jinn unless they have sexual intercourse with her. She demands their royal rings as tokens and shows them her large collection of rings, given to her by other one-time lovers.
The brothers decide that the jinn is even more miserable than them and return to their kingdoms.  Shahriyâr has his wife and the slaves killed. In his bitterness, he decides that all women are the same. Shahriyâr begins to marry a new virgin every day, only to execute each one the next morning, before she has a chance to dishonor him.
Eventually, the Vizier, whose duty it is to provide them, cannot find any more virgins. Shahrazad, the vizier's daughter, offers herself as the next bride and her father reluctantly agrees. On the night of their marriage, Shahrazâd asks the king to have her sister Dinarzad join her. Then Dinarzad  asked her sister to tell one of her wonderful stories. Shahrazad start telling one tale (The Fisherman and the jinni), but does not end it. The king, curious about how the story ends, is thus forced to postpone her execution in order to hear the conclusion. The next night, as soon as she finishes the tale, she begins another one, and the king, eager to hear the conclusion of that tale as well, postpones her execution once again. This goes on for one thousand and one nights, hence the name.


The Tales

The number and order of the stories varies from manuscript to manuscript, to edition and edition and from translation to translation. Nowadays, the overall corpus comprises more than 550 tales from various genres and sizes.
The genre of tales vary widely: they include historical tales, love stories, tragedies, comedies, poems, burlesques, and various forms of erotica. Numerous stories depict jinn, ghouls, ape people, sorcerers, magicians, and legendary places, which are often intermingled with real people and geography, not always rationally. Common protagonists include the historical Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid, his Grand Vizier, Jafar al-Barmaki, and the famous poet Abu Nuwas, despite the fact that these figures lived some 200 years after the fall of the Sassanid Empire, in which the frame tale of Scheherazade is set. Some tales even present late medieval rulers as Baybars or Timur, or go into mythic pre-islamic time. Sometimes a character in Scheherazade's tale will begin telling other characters a story of their own, and that story may have another one told within it, resulting in a richly layered narrative texture.


Conclusion
Different variants of the conclusion agree that the king Shahriyâr gave his wife Shahrazad a pardon at the end and spared her life. They differ in the details:

After a thousand nights, Shahrazad gave birth to a child and presented it to her husband, explaining the stratagem she had employed to save her life. The king admired her undertaking, became attached to her, and decided to spare her. Dinarzad, the king's qahramāna (female steward), had assisted the queen in carrying out her plan. (According to the earliest known summary, recorded by Ibn al-Nadīm in his tenth-century Fihrist.)
During the 1001 nights, Shahrazad bore the king three children. (The standard ending found in the nineteenth-century printed editions of the ZER recension.)
After the story of Maruf the Cobbler, King Shahriyār  grew tired of Shahrazad's storytelling and ordered her execution for the following morning. Shahrazad therefore sent for their three children and asked the king to spare her life, a request he granted. (According to Von Hammer's ZER manuscript, dating from the early nineteenth century)
After Shahrazad had finished telling all the stories she knew, Shahriyār recognized her intelligence and resourcefulness. Since she had also borne him two children, he decided to spare her life. The following morning, he bestowed numerous favors upon her father, the vizier. They all continued to live together until their deaths. (According to the so-called Mystified Sabbagh Manuscript, dating from the early nineteenth century.)
Some manuscripts said to be "complete" contain no ending sequence at all. (Like the Wortley Montague Manuscript, dating from the eighteenth century.)
A more elaborate ending depicts Shahrazad gradually reforming the king through stories that encourage him to reflect on his own circumstances and question whether executing his former wives had been justified.  After the final story cycle (Baybars and the Sixteeen Captains of Police, or The Craft and Malice of women) Shahrazad begins recounting the frame story of the Nights itself, presenting it to the king in a modified form and without mentioning the characters' names. Shahriyār eventually recognizes that the story mirrors his own and acknowledges that he deserved God's punishment for his actions. He thanks God for sending Shahrazad to guide him back to the right path. Shahrazad then instructs him on the relationship between a ruler and his army, as well as between a ruler and his subjects. She also relates two additional stories about unfaithful concubines, demonstrating to the king that his predicament was not unique and that other kings had experienced similar situations. Fully convinced of his wrongdoing and of Shahrazad's unparalleled wisdom, the king arranges a splendid double wedding: he marries Shahrazad, while his brother, Shāhzamān, marries Dinarzad.(Shāhzamān had been wedding and killing girls as well) Shahrazad's tales are subsequently compiled into a book entitled One Thousand and One Nights. (According to the Kayseri family of manuscripts, dating from the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries, and the Breslau edition. Galland is also thought to have heard of this ending.)
After the tale of Harun ar-Rashid and The Merchant of Oman,Shahrazad begins recounting the frame story. In  this embedded tale, the "unnamed queen" had been pregnant three times, although the "unnamed king was unaware of the pregnancies.When the king asks to see his sons, they are brought before him. The narrative then returns to Shahrazad and Shahriyār.  Shahrazad explains that a woman's worth lies in her intelligence and faith, and asks her sister Dinarzad to bring her three children before the king. Shahriyār is delighted to see them. (According to the  late Reinhardt Manuscript, dating from the nineteenth century).


History, versions and translations
There is no single canonical text of the Nights with a fixed number of stories in a fixed order.
The text's history is complex. Scholars have made many attempts to untangle how extant collections came about. Robert Irwin summarises their findings:

In the 1880s and 1890s a lot of work was done on the Nights by Zotenberg and others, in the course of which a consensus view of the history of the text emerged. Most scholars agreed that the Nights was a composite work and that the earliest tales in it came from India and Persia. At some time, probably in the early eighth century, these tales were translated into Arabic under the title Alf Layla, or 'The Thousand Nights'. This collection then formed the basis of The Thousand and One Nights. The original core of stories was quite small. Then, in Iraq in the ninth or tenth century, this original core had Arab stories added to it—among them some tales about the Caliph Harun al-Rashid. Also, perhaps from the tenth century onwards, previously independent sagas and story cycles were added to the compilation [...] Then, from the 13th century onwards, a further layer of stories was added in Syria and Egypt, many of these showing a preoccupation with sex, magic or low life. In the early modern period yet more stories were added to the Egyptian collections so as to swell the bulk of the text sufficiently to bring its length up to the full 1,001 nights of storytelling promised by the book's title.


Possible Indian influence
Devices found in Sanskrit literature such as frame stories and animal fables are seen by some scholars as lying at the root of the conception of the Nights.
Emmanuel Cosquin (1909) argued that various narrative elements of the frame story of the Nights had origins in ancient Indian literature: (1) A husband who discovers his wife's infidelity and falls into profound grief. he later recovers his joy when he witnesses the fact that a person  from a higher social rank is struck by the same misfortune. It appears in the third-century Chinese Tripitaka, a translation of a lost Indian source. (2) A woman deceives her master, who holded her captive in a trunk; while he is fast asleep, she has sexual intercourse with other men. grok_lead: One Thousand and One Nights, also known as Arabian Nights, is a renowned collection of Middle Eastern and South Asian folk tales compiled in Arabic during the Islamic Golden Age, spanning roughly the 8th to 14th centuries. The narrative framework centers on Scheherazade (or Shahrazad), the clever daughter of the king's vizier, who volunteers to marry the tyrannical King Shahryar after he vows to execute a new bride each day following his betrayal by his first wife. To postpone her death, Scheherazade recounts enthralling stories night after night, each left unfinished at dawn to ensure her survival, ultimately spanning 1,001 nights and leading to the king's redemption. This structure weaves together hundreds of tales featuring genies, merchants, caliphs, and mythical creatures, blending elements of adventure, romance, fantasy, and moral lessons. The origins of One Thousand and One Nights trace back to the early 9th century, with the oldest surviving fragmentâa Syrian paper manuscriptâdiscovered in 1948 and dated to around that period, providing evidence of its early circulation in the Abbasid era. It was first documented in the 10th-century catalog Fihrist by Ibn al-Nadim, which lists it among works of storytellers and includes a brief description of the frame tale. Over centuries, the collection evolved through oral traditions and written compilations in regions like Baghdad, Syria, and Egypt, incorporating influences from Persian, Indian, Greek, Turkish, and Central Asian sources, resulting in a fluid text with no single definitive version. The first printed Arabic edition appeared in 1835 from the Bulaq Press in Cairo, standardizing a version that included both ancient core stories and later additions. Notable tales within the collection include the voyages of Sinbad the Sailor, encounters with jinn and magical objects, and intricate plots involving trickery and justice, often nested within one another to create a labyrinthine structure. Themes of fate, divine intervention, gender roles, and the power of storytelling recur throughout, reflecting the diverse cultural mosaic of the Islamic world and pre-Islamic folklore. Some iconic stories, such as Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp and Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves, were actually introduced in Antoine Galland's early 18th-century French translation, drawing from oral sources rather than the medieval Arabic manuscripts. The work's global reception began with Galland's partial translation (1704â1717), which ignited European fascination and shaped Orientalist perceptions of the East through its exoticism and sensuality. Later, Sir Richard Burton's unexpurgated 16-volume English edition (1885â1888) further disseminated the tales, preserving their linguistic and cultural nuances while sparking debates on censorship and authenticity. One Thousand and One Nights has profoundly influenced literature, theater, music, and film worldwide, inspiring adaptations from Mozart's operas to Disney animations, and underscoring the enduring appeal of its narrative ingenuity.
